summary: The article examines the growing conversation about inclusivity in community theater casting as autumn productions launch. It argues that stages should mirror their communities, that "culture-conscious casting" goes beyond color-blind casting, and that diversity must be substantive rather than tokenistic. Examples from several local theaters illustrate intentional, community-driven approaches, framed as both a moral and artistic imperative.
one_line: Community theaters are moving beyond color-blind casting toward intentional, culture-conscious inclusivity, which is framed as both a moral and artistic imperative.
key_facts: Sarah Langston, a seasoned director with the Midtown Players, says "Our stage should serve as a mirror to society" and calls inclusivity "not just good ethics, it's good art."
Riverside Repertory has adopted "culture-conscious casting" since October 2023, going beyond color-blind casting.
Tyrone Greene, Artistic Director at Riverside Repertory, says culture-conscious casting means actively embracing an actor's race or ethnicity rather than ignoring it.
In fall 2023 the Coastal Curtain Collective held open auditions for "Romeo and Juliet" and cast Maria Vasquez, an Afro-Latina actor, and wheelchair user Jacob Newman in the leading roles.
Coastal Curtain director Emma Thompson said seeing Maria and Jacob on stage was powerful for everyone because "it embodied the reality of our world."
The article defines tokenism as making only a symbolic effort to be inclusive, such as casting a single actor of color in an otherwise homogenous cast.
The Elmsfield Theatre Ensemble began an inclusivity effort in September 2023 aimed at reflecting the actual demographics of its community.
Nadia Khan, a Pakistani-American actress and regular on the Elmsfield stage, says intentional, substantive diversity acknowledges performers' presence in the community and enriches storytelling.
Harmony Hall Community Theater opened in late 2023 and held workshops and discussions with community leaders and activists before its inaugural season.
Lee Chen, a founding member of Harmony Hall, says "It's about listening and then acting."
The article argues the moral imperative is justice and fairness, removing systemic barriers for non-white, non-able-bodied, and non-heteronormative individuals, so talent is the only criterion.
The artistic argument is that a diversified cast offers a multiplicity of perspectives and adds layers of meaning that can resonate with a broader audience.
